legal.summary: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani of the Bombay High Court has stated that compelling parties into mediation is counterproductive and should be avoided. The judge made this observation while hearing a case, emphasizing that mediation is effective only when both parties genuinely consent and are willing to negotiate in good faith. Forcing unwilling parties into a mediation process, Bhambhani noted, wastes judicial resources and rarely produces settlement outcomes. The comment reflects growing concern among Indian judges about the efficacy of mandatory mediation schemes, particularly in commercial and civil disputes. The judgment underscores a tension between court-ordered ADR mechanisms intended to decongest dockets and the practical reality that coerced participation often fails. This statement carries weight given recent emphasis on mediation under the Indian Legal Services Authority framework and court-annexed mediation rules across high courts.
legal.contextNote: This reflects judicial skepticism of mandatory mediation mandates under Rules 32 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (as amended), and court-annexed mediation schemes introduced by various high courts post-2016. The statement does not cite specific precedent but aligns with concerns raised in *Afcons Infrastructure Ltd v. Chore House Ventures Pvt Ltd* (2019, SC) regarding ADR efficacy. For in-house counsel: (1) document client consent to mediation explicitly — courts may now scrutinize whether participation was truly voluntary before enforcing settlement agreements; (2) expect judges to be less aggressive in stay-of-suit orders on the ground of pending mediation, particularly if the opposing party has signaled unwillingness; (3) review your firm's mediation clauses in contracts — passive language ('subject to mediation') may not survive judicial pressure to abandon forced mediation tracks in litigation.

legal.headline: CCPA: Rapido’s pre-ride tipping prompts misleading and unfair; ₹10 lakh penalty imposed
legal.hook: Holding that Rapido’s pre-ride tipping prompts misled consumers into believing that additional payments would improve ride availability and confirmation, the CCPA found the practice to constitute misleading…

The regulator found that Rapido's prompts mislead consumers into believing that offering additional payments before confirming a ride would improve availability and faster ride confirmation. The CCPA classified the practice as both a misleading advertisement (violating the Consumer Protection Act, 2019) and an unfair trade practice, and specifically identified it as a prohibited dark pattern—a structural design choice that exploits cognitive biases or information asymmetries to nudge users toward economically suboptimal decisions. The order does not specify when the tipping feature was introduced or removed, or whether Rapido has been directed to alter its app UI prospectively.
legal.contextNote: This invokes Section 2(47) (unfair trade practice), Section 10 (misleading advertisements), and Schedule II of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which now defines dark patterns as a regulatory category. CCPA (2023 SCC OnLine Del 1919)* on deceptive bundling is analogous. (1) In-house counsel for ride-hailing, fintech, and marketplace platforms should audit pre-transaction prompts, consent flows, and default settings for any mechanism that conditions service quality on discretionary consumer outlay; CCPA treats UI design itself as conduct.
